newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa begins destruction of landmine stockpile.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa begins destruction of landmine stockpile.

text.p: South Africa began destroying its stockpile of anti-personnel landmines on Wednesday, but said it would continue to develop anti-tank mines.
By October the South African National Defence Force (SANDF) will have destroyed all its anti-personnel landmines in 10 explosions.
"Over the next six months the SANDF will destroy 261,423 anti-personnel landmines," Defence Minister Joe Modise told officials at the Alkantpan weapons test range in the north of the country.
"These will be destroyed by explosives and those anti-personnel landmines made mainly of plastic will be dismantled so that the plastic is recycled," he added.
South Africa banned the use, development, production and stockpiling of anti-personnel mines in February to support a 1980 United Nations convention.
Before detonating the first 4,700 landmines on Wednesday, Modise said the military would keep about 5,000 active mines to help develop demining techniques.
He told Reuters the stockpiles would include about 8,000 foreign-made landmines collected during South Africa's covert operations in Angola during the 1980s.
"I can assure the world that never again will landmines be produced in this country for the purpose of war," Modise said.
Later however he told Reuters that South Africa was continuing the development of an anti-tank mine.
"We also have a country to defend," Modise said.
"We are looking at a 'smart' anti-tank mine which will destroy itself... They will only be placed in areas where there is actual combat -- not where there are civilians."
Southern Africa is the world's most heavily mined region, with an estimated 20 million mines, of which just 400,000 have been removed since 1991.
Although many governments in the region have called for a ban on anti-personnel mines, only South Africa and Mozambique have officially banned their use.
